statement: Contemporary K'iche' and broader highland Guatemalan Maya religious practice has documented restricted-knowledge/initiation conventions centered on the ajq'ij ("daykeeper") role — practitioners of the 260-day sacred calendar (Tzolkʼin-descended) who undergo multi-year training/oral apprenticeship and function as living custodians of ritual knowledge. Ajqʼijabʼ (plural) practiced this role in secrecy during Guatemala's civil war (1960-1996) due to persecution, becoming more publicly visible only after the 1996 peace accords. Per this project's ethical constraint, this claim reports the existence of this restricted-knowledge tradition and its documented persecution history only; no ceremonial content is described.

sources.citation: General secondary sourcing on contemporary Maya spirituality and the ajqʼij role (ResearchGate-indexed material and a Penn Museum Expedition magazine piece; full author/journal citations not fully extracted in this research pass).
